concept_html:
Git integration connects a Fabric workspace to a branch and folder in a Git repository. Supported providers are Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitHub Enterprise, all cloud-based only. Some item types are still in preview, so check the supported-items list for each one you use (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026).

What Git holds. Item definitions, not data. Each item gets its own folder of definition files. For a lakehouse, Git tracks metadata only: its name, shortcuts and OneLake security roles. Tables and files are not tracked, and Git operations never overwrite them. Rebuilding a workspace from Git gives you empty lakehouses. Your pipelines must reload the data.

Two directions:

  • Commit exports workspace changes to the branch.
  • Update imports branch changes into the workspace and overwrites the workspace version.

The source control panel shows each item's state. If an item changed in both places, you have a conflict to resolve before you continue.

Who does what. Only a workspace Admin connects or disconnects the workspace. Members and Contributors commit and update, limited by their permissions in the Git repository. Viewers see no Git information.

One workspace, one branch. A workspace is a shared runtime. Anything one person changes there affects everyone using it. Microsoft's recommended pattern is a separate workspace per developer, each connected to its own feature branch. You develop in your workspace, commit to your branch, and open a pull request into the main branch. The shared workspace connected to main then updates from Git.

Alternatively, develop in client tools such as VS Code for notebooks or Power BI Desktop for reports, and push to your branch.

Keep notebooks small and parameterised, and keep configuration in files your pipeline reads. Reviewers read diffs. A 900-line notebook with hard-coded paths produces diffs nobody can review.

exercises.prompt: Your team's rule for the source control panel: resolve conflicts first, then commit your changes, then update from Git. Write `next_step(statuses: dict[str, str]) -> str`. Values are `"synced"`, `"uncommitted"`, `"update_required"` or `"conflict"`. Return `"resolve"` if any item is in conflict, else `"commit"` if any is uncommitted, else `"update"` if any needs an update, else `"none"`. Raise `ValueError` for an unknown status. Use a constant for the allowed statuses.
exercises.prompt_html: Your team's rule for the source control panel: resolve conflicts first, then commit your changes, then update from Git. Write next_step(statuses: dict[str, str]) -> str. Values are "synced", "uncommitted", "update_required" or "conflict". Return "resolve" if any item is in conflict, else "commit" if any is uncommitted, else "update" if any needs an update, else "none". Raise ValueError for an unknown status. Use a constant for the allowed statuses.
exercises.solution:
ALLOWED_STATUSES = frozenset({"synced", "uncommitted", "update_required", "conflict"})


def next_step(statuses: dict[str, str]) -> str:
    """Next source control action for a workspace.

    Args:
        statuses: Item name to source control status.

    Returns:
        "resolve", "commit", "update" or "none".

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a status is not recognised.
    """
    present = set(statuses.values())
    unknown = present - ALLOWED_STATUSES
    if unknown:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown statuses: {sorted(unknown)}")
    if "conflict" in present:
        return "resolve"
    if "uncommitted" in present:
        return "commit"
    if "update_required" in present:
        return "update"
    return "none"

title: Git integration for Fabric workspaces
why_html: Three engineers shared one development workspace connected to main. One of them updated from Git while another had an hour of uncommitted notebook edits. The update overwrote the workspace version, and the edits were lost. With a workspace and branch per developer, each person's work stays isolated until it merges.
